h1: Nervous System Regulation Is Not About Becoming Less
intro: What if the goal was never to calm yourself down, but to become capable of holding more of who you are?

So much of what we hear about nervous system regulation centers on calm, and for good reason. True calm is one of the most healing energies we have. In Internal Family Systems, calm is one of the qualities of Self: the loving, spacious presence at the core of who we are. From that kind of calm, the nervous system can come to ground and recalibrate, and the authentic self has room to emerge.
What I gently set aside is a different kind of "calm": the pressure to quiet down, smooth over, and be less. That isn't regulation. It's another way of making ourselves smaller.

To me, nervous system regulation is the growing capacity to stay in relationship with yourself through a wider range of human experience. To feel fear without being run by it. To feel anger without suppressing it or letting it take over. To feel desire, grief, joy, and intensity, and stay present enough to listen to what they carry.
This page explores what nervous system regulation is, how to regulate your nervous system in ways that fit what you actually need, and a few simple somatic exercises you can start with today.

blocks.text: Your nervous system is constantly asking one question beneath your awareness: Am I safe right now?

Based on the answer, it shifts your whole body into a different state. When it senses safety, you can rest, connect, think clearly, play, and create. When it senses threat, it mobilizes you to fight or flee. When the threat feels too big to escape, it may shut you down: numbness, collapse, fog, disconnection. And when belonging feels at risk, it may move you to appease, accommodate, and please.
None of these states are wrong. Each one is your body's intelligence, trying to keep you alive and connected.

Nervous system regulation is the capacity to move through these states and return to a felt sense of safety and connection. Not to stay calm forever, but to come back. To have more choice about where you go, and how long you stay there.

When we talk about someone being "dysregulated," we usually mean they have lost access to that return. Their system is stuck in high alert, or stuck in shutdown, or swinging between the two, often long after the original danger has passed.
The good news is that regulation is a capacity, not a fixed trait. It can be built, practiced, and strengthened, especially in relationship.

sections.heading: Regulation Is About Capacity, Not Becoming Less

blocks.text: Regulation isn't about controlling what we feel. It's about having enough steady, spacious presence to stay with ourselves through the full range of human experience: grief, fear, anger, desire, joy.

For many people, especially women, this lands on an old wound. We already learned to be agreeable, easy, and small. We learned that our fire was too much. A version of regulation that asks us to keep smoothing ourselves down can become one more way of exiling the parts of us that most need to come home.
I think of it differently.

In my work, I think about two territories: the wound and the wildness. The wound is what happened to you, and it often needs settling, tending, and safety. The wildness is the anger, passion, voice, and life force that learned it wasn't welcome, and it often needs room, movement, and expression.
A regulated nervous system can hold both.
From that place of presence, I invite you to ask:

items: Can I feel this activation without being consumed by it?
Can I notice fear without automatically organizing my life around avoiding it?
Can I let anger inform me without suppressing it or letting it take over?
Can I feel desire without immediately judging it?
Can I stay present with intensity and get curious about what it carries?

blocks.text: That is regulation as capacity. In a loving, spacious calm, there is room for all of it: the tenderness and the fire. Not becoming less. Becoming able to inhabit more of who you are.

sections.heading: Signs Your Nervous System Is Asking for Support

blocks.text: A nervous system that has been working hard for a long time often speaks through patterns like these:
When it's stuck on high alert

items: Feeling wired, restless, or unable to switch off
Irritability or anger that seems bigger than the moment
Scanning for what might go wrong

blocks.text: When it's moved toward shutdown

items: Numbness, fog, or feeling far away from yourself
Losing access to what you want or feel

blocks.text: When it's organizing around belonging

items: Losing your own signals when someone else is upset
Saying yes when your body is saying no

blocks.text: These are not character flaws. They are protective strategies that once made sense. Fight, flight, freeze, and fawn are the body's intelligence at work. They become exhausting only when they keep running long after they're needed.
A system that has been working this hard needs help. And deserves it.
If these patterns feel overwhelming, or you are in crisis, please reach out to a licensed mental health professional or call or text 988 in the US.

sections.heading: How to Regulate Your Nervous System: Different Tools for Different Jobs

blocks.text: Most nervous system regulation techniques are taught as if every body needs the same thing. Breathe deeply. Slow down. But a system stuck in shutdown doesn't need more slowing. And a system on fire may not be ready to sit still.
Regulation starts with a simple question: What is this moment asking for?

rows: Longer exhales, orienting to your surroundings, feeling your feet and seat
Small movements, stretching, standing, cool water on your hands, stepping outside
Pushing against a wall, shaking, walking briskly, voicing a sound, writing it out
Reaching out to a safe person, placing a hand on your heart, naming one thing you want
Warmth, slowness, being witnessed, letting tears come

blocks.text: There is no single correct volume for aliveness. Sometimes your nervous system needs settling. Sometimes it needs movement. Sometimes it needs protection, rest, expression, connection, grief, or play.
The skill isn't memorizing techniques. It's developing enough relationship with your body to discern what this particular moment needs, and offering it.

sections.heading: 5 Somatic Exercises for Nervous System Regulation

blocks.text: These simple nervous system regulation exercises take a few minutes or less. Go slowly. Stop anything that doesn't feel right, and notice what changes, even slightly.

items.text: Orienting: let your eyes tell your body where you are. Slowly turn your head and let your eyes land on whatever draws them: a color, a window, a plant. Take your time. Let your body register that you are here, now, in this room. Notice whether your breath or shoulders shift.
items.goodFor: Good for: anxiety, bracing, feeling stuck in the past.

items.text: The longer exhale. Breathe in naturally. Let the exhale be a little longer than the inhale, like a slow sigh. Repeat five or six times. No forcing.
items.goodFor: Good for: settling a revved-up system.

items.text: Feet, seat, ground. Feel the weight of your feet on the floor and your body on the chair. Press your feet down gently and notice the ground pressing back. Let yourself be held by something solid.
items.goodFor: Good for: overwhelm, spinning thoughts, feeling ungrounded.

items.text: Push and press: giving the fire somewhere to go. Stand facing a wall and press into it with both palms, as if pushing it away. Feel the strength in your arms, back, and legs. Hold for a few breaths, then release. Notice what's left.
items.goodFor: Good for: anger, frustration, intensity that wants to move.

items.text: Hand on heart, one true thing. Place a hand on your chest or belly. Feel the warmth. Silently name one true thing: I'm scared. I'm tired. I want more. Let it be true without fixing it.

blocks.text: These practices are a starting place, not a cure. Many people find their nervous system learns safety most deeply in relationship, with someone steady beside them. That's what somatic coaching offers. Learn about somatic coaching →
Long before we had breathing techniques, we had the natural world.

The rhythm of waves. Wind moving through leaves. The slow arc of the sun. Our nervous systems evolved in conversation with these patterns, and many people find their bodies settle faster outdoors than anywhere else.

Nature also models something regulation advice often forgets: there is intensity everywhere. Storms, volcanoes, rushing rivers, the insistent push of a seed breaking open underground. Nature has never asked life to be one volume. It moves through expansion and contraction, eruption and rest.
If you can, take one of the exercises above outside. Let your eyes find the horizon. Let the ground hold you.

sections.heading: Nervous System Healing Happens in Relationship

blocks.text: Most of what wounds us happens in relationship. So it makes sense that much of our nervous system healing happens there too.

We learn regulation first by borrowing it, from a caregiver's calm voice or a steady presence that tells our body the danger has passed. When that wasn't available, or wasn't consistent, the capacity didn't get to fully develop. It can still develop now. A steady, attuned relationship gives your nervous system something to lean on while it learns.

sections.heading: Regulation Is the Ground of Self-Trust

blocks.text: Here is the thread running through all of my work: self-trust is built in the body.

You can know in your mind that you're allowed to want things, set boundaries, and take up space, and still find your body bracing, freezing, or abandoning you the moment it matters. Self-trust can't hold if your nervous system treats your own needs as danger.

As regulation grows, something shifts. You can stay with yourself when fear shows up. You can feel discomfort and still move toward what matters, which is the heart of psychological flexibility. And you begin to discern the difference between a signal that says stop and the discomfort of stepping beyond an old pattern.
That is when self-trust stops being an idea and becomes something you can actually feel.

faqs.question: What is nervous system regulation?
faqs.answer: Nervous system regulation is the capacity to move through states of activation and shutdown and return to a felt sense of safety and connection. It isn't about forcing calm or making yourself smaller. It's about having more choice and more capacity to stay present with yourself.

faqs.question: How do I regulate my nervous system quickly?
faqs.answer: Start by noticing what your body needs. If you're revved up, try a longer exhale or orienting to your surroundings. If you're numb or foggy, try gentle movement or stepping outside. Small, simple practices done often tend to work better than big efforts done rarely.

faqs.question: What are signs of a dysregulated nervous system?
faqs.answer: Common signs include feeling constantly on edge, trouble switching off, irritability, numbness or fog, exhaustion that rest doesn't fix, and automatically pleasing others at your own expense.

faqs.question: How long does nervous system healing take?
faqs.answer: It varies. Many people feel small shifts within weeks of regular practice, while deeper patterns often change over months. Building capacity is gradual, and it tends to grow faster with consistent support.

faqs.question: Can a coach help with nervous system regulation?
faqs.answer: Yes. A somatic coach can help you learn your body's signals, practice regulation in real time, and build capacity at your pace. Somatic coaching is not therapy and does not treat trauma or mental health conditions. If you need clinical care, please seek a licensed professional.

closing: You don't have to become less to feel safe.
If you're ready to build a nervous system that can hold more of who you are, let's talk. The first conversation is free, 20 minutes, and online.
